question: Can a player in the K-armed bandit problem guarantee low regret against the best arm, any sequence of arms, or the best of N experts when rewards are chosen by an adversary with no statistical assumptions?
hypothesis: Randomised exponential-weight algorithms with importance-weighted reward estimates achieve O(sqrt(T)) worst-case regret with only logarithmic dependence on the number of experts (stated aims, proved by theorems).
contributions: Exp3 and Exp3.1: expected weak regret O(sqrt(K T ln K)), the latter uniform over T
Lower bound Omega(sqrt(KT)) for any algorithm
Exp3.P and Exp3.P.1: weak regret bound holding with probability 1-delta and with probability 1
Exp4: regret against best of N experts O(sqrt(K T ln N))
Exp3.S: regret against arbitrary action sequences, scaled by their hardness
Application: Hannan-consistency and convergence to minimax value in unknown repeated games

results.claim: Exp3.P.1 is Hannan-consistent in the unknown repeated-game setup; Theorem 9.1 gives high-probability regret rate equal to the Theorem 6.4 bound divided by T, optimal in T and K up to log factors. Theorem 9.3: with Exp3.1 on unknown payoff matrix in [a,b]^{n x m}, row player's expected per-round payoff >= v - 8 sqrt(e-1) sqrt(n ln n / T) - 8(e-1) n/T - 2 n ln n/T.

limits: Exp3 upper bound sqrt(K T ln K) and lower bound sqrt(K T)/20 differ by a sqrt(ln K) factor; closing it is stated as an open problem (p.12).
Exp3 needs an upper bound g on Gmax (or T) for tuning; Exp3.1, Exp3.P.1, Exp3.S.1 remove this by restarts at the cost of larger constants.
Exp3.P requires T as input; its probability bound holds only for delta >= K T e^{-KT} and T >= (20/3) K ln K (WLOG assumption).
Exp4 needs the uniform expert in (or in the convex hull of) the expert set; it runs in time linear in N per round.
Rewards are in [0,1]; other ranges by rescaling.
Section 9 extends results to adaptive adversaries (game play) but the authors leave checking that all results hold 'to the interested reader'.

Regret is weak regret against a fixed best arm; bounds do not compete with the O(ln T) stochastic rates of Lai and Robbins, and the authors say the gap is due to quantification order (reward distribution fixed vs depending on T), not adversarial setting.
No experiments or implementation in the paper; all results are theorems with explicit constants.

code.snippet: p_i(t) = (1-gamma) w_i(t)/sum_j w_j(t) + gamma/K;  xhat_j(t) = x_j(t)/p_j(t) if j=i_t else 0;  w_j(t+1) = w_j(t) exp(gamma xhat_j(t)/K);  w_i(1)=1
Exp3.S update: w_j(t+1) = w_j(t) exp(gamma xhat_j(t)/K) + (e*alpha/K) sum_i w_i(t)
